overview.historicalContext:
The impossibility of dissecting a cube into smaller cubes of all different sizes was proved by J.E. Littlewood and included in his book 'A Mathematician's Miscellany' (1953) as an example of mathematical elegance. The proof requires no computation or algebraic manipulation — just geometric visualization and infinite descent.

The 2D analog has a completely different answer: a square CAN be dissected into squares of all different sizes. The first such 'squared square' was found by Brooks, Smith, Stone, and Tutte in 1940, using an ingenious connection to electrical network theory. The smallest 'simple perfect squared square' has 21 squares and side 112, found by Duijvestijn (1978).

The key geometric reason for the dimensional difference: in 3D, the smallest cube on any floor is completely surrounded by taller cubes on all 4 sides, forcing its top face to be a new interior floor. In 2D, a square can extend to the boundary wall, breaking the descent argument. The impossibility extends to all dimensions >= 3 and to rectangular boxes.
overview.problemStatement:
**Theorem (Littlewood)**: A cube cannot be dissected into a finite number of smaller cubes, all of different sizes.

Equivalently: In any dissection of a cube into finitely many smaller cubes, at least two cubes must have the same size.

This is Wiedijk's 100 Theorems #82.
overview.proofStrategy:
**Littlewood's Proof by Infinite Descent**:

1. Consider the bottom face of the large cube, covered by smaller cubes
2. Find the smallest cube touching the bottom — call it C (via `Finset.exists_min_image`)
3. Since all sizes differ, C is surrounded by taller cubes on all sides
4. C's top face becomes a new 'floor' at a higher level
5. This floor is covered by cubes smaller than C
6. Repeat: generates an infinite strictly decreasing sequence of cube sizes
7. A strictly decreasing chain of length n requires n distinct cubes (injectivity via `Fintype.card_le_of_injective`)
8. Take a chain of length card+1 > card — contradiction with finiteness (`omega`)
keyInsights: The infinite descent argument requires no computation — pure geometric reasoning
The 2D case (squaring the square) IS possible because edge squares can reach the boundary, breaking the surrounding argument
The key geometric step (3D surrounding) is axiomatized: the smallest cube on any floor has its top face as a new interior floor
The proved `chain_length_bounded` lemma reduces the problem to pigeonhole: a strictly decreasing chain is injective, so its length is bounded by the number of cubes
The impossibility generalizes to all dimensions >= 3 and to dissection of rectangular boxes

sections.mathContext: Strictly decreasing chain of length $n$ is injective $\implies n \leq |\text{cubes}|$. Proof: $\text{chain}(i) \neq \text{chain}(j)$ for $i < j$ since sizes differ; then `Fintype.card_le_of_injective`.

sections.mathContext: 2D: 'squared square' exists (Brooks-Smith-Stone-Tutte 1940, smallest: 21 squares, side 112). 3D: impossible by Littlewood's descent. The dimensional barrier: 3D cubes are surrounded on all sides; 2D squares can reach the boundary.

conclusion.summary: Littlewood's proof elegantly shows that cube dissection into different-sized cubes is impossible through infinite descent. The smallest cube on any 'floor' creates a new floor above it with even smaller cubes, leading to infinitely many cubes — contradicting finiteness. The proof is remarkably short: the main theorem is just 3 lines of Lean + omega.
conclusion.implications:
The 2D analog (squaring the square) IS possible — the first solution (1940) had 69 squares, the smallest simple one has 21 squares
The impossibility extends to all dimensions >= 3 and to rectangular boxes
The proof pattern (infinite descent via pigeonhole on chain length) appears in Erdős-Szekeres, Ramsey theory, and Dilworth's theorem
The axiomatized geometric covering step (smaller_cube_above) is the remaining gap — it requires formal 3D tiling theory
openQuestions: Minimum number of repeated sizes needed in a cube dissection
Generalizations to other 3D shapes (e.g., can a tetrahedron be dissected into tetrahedra of all different sizes?)
Formalizing the geometric covering axiom (smaller_cube_above) without external axioms
Connections to packing problems and the Dehn invariant

crossReferences.description: Both are impossibility results in mathematics: the dissection of cubes shows no finite decomposition into distinct smaller cubes exists, while Hilbert's 10th shows no algorithm solves all Diophantine equations

Both are impossibility results in geometry: angle trisection shows certain constructions are impossible with compass and straightedge, while cube dissection shows certain geometric decompositions are impossible
